paper.title: Fast Catch-Up, Late Switching: Optimal Batch Size Scheduling via Functional Scaling Laws

read: full text (arXiv HTML): Sections 1-6 and Appendix B (LLM and linear-regression setups, catch-up, switching-time and late-switch details, learning-rate-schedule interaction); Appendix A (proofs) skimmed

claims.claim: For one-pass SGD with a constant learning rate on linear regression whose features and target have power-law spectra, the best batch-size schedule for a fixed data budget depends on task difficulty: on easy tasks the batch should grow throughout training, while on hard tasks it should stay at the minimum for almost all of training and grow only in a short final phase, and either schedule reaches the best rate one-pass SGD can achieve without decaying the learning rate. Supported only if discrete SGD runs using the derived schedules show final loss scaling with data size at the predicted minimax rate D^(-s*beta/(1+s*beta)) in an easy-task setting and at D^(-s) in a hard-task setting; if, restricted to two-stage schedules, the optimal switch for hard tasks comes after nearly all the data with the remaining fraction shrinking as a power of D; and if a constant learning rate with such a schedule matches cosine and warmup-stable-decay learning-rate schedules in final loss.
claims.decision_rule: Simulated SGD final loss matches D^(-s*beta/(1+s*beta)) (s=1, beta=2) and D^(-s) (s=0.4, beta=2); two-stage optimum late with (D-P*)/D -> 0 as power law; constant LR + BSS ~ cosine/WSD.

claims.claim: In language-model pretraining, when the batch size is raised from small to large, the loss quickly falls onto the curve of a run that used the large batch all along, so the switch can be deferred until late in training: under a fixed token budget, a late switch beats both an early switch and constant batch sizes. Supported only if, for dense models (50M-0.5B) and mixture-of-experts models (1B on 0.4T tokens, 1.1B on 1T tokens), the switched run's loss merges with the constant-large-batch run soon after every switch, including each step of a multi-stage schedule; if late switching gives lower final validation loss than early switching in every configuration tested; if the best switch for a 200M model falls well past the middle of training; and if the optimal remaining-data amount D - P* follows a power law in D with R^2 at least 0.95.
claims.decision_rule: Catch-up visible after each switch in all configs; late switch < early switch final loss in all; optimal switch fraction > 0.5 (paper ~0.7); log(D - P*) vs log D linear fit R^2 >= 0.95.

experiments.text: Set up the theory. Setup: one-pass SGD on feature-space linear regression with power-law capacity exponent beta and source exponent s, approximated by an SDE whose loss follows a functional scaling law: excess risk = T^(-s) (signal learning in intrinsic time T) + an integral of a forgetting kernel over noise injected at rate eta*sigma^2 / b(t). Minimise final loss over the schedule b(t) and horizon T subject to total data D = integral of b(t) and b(t) >= B_min. Result (theorems): easy tasks (s >= 1 - 1/beta) favour b(t) ~ B_max (T - t + 1)^(-gamma) growing throughout; hard tasks favour B_min for all but a vanishing fraction (T - T1)/T ~ D^(-(1-1/beta-s)/(2-1/beta)) of training, with loss ~ D^(-s); in the two-stage class, easy tasks prefer the large batch throughout and hard tasks a late switch with D - P* ~ D^gamma.

Check the predicted rates with discrete SGD. Setup: easy task s = 1, beta = 2 and hard task s = 0.4, beta = 2, sigma = 1, learning rate 5e-4, schedules built from the theorem and discretised, data sizes 6,346-137,693. Result: final loss against D follows D^(-s*beta/(1+s*beta)) in the easy regime and D^(-s) in the hard regime (shown on log-log plots); with s = 0.3, beta = 1.5, the theorem-derived schedule at constant learning rate gives a final loss comparable to cosine and warmup-stable-decay schedules (figure).

Explain fast catch-up with the scaling law. Setup: two-stage schedule from B1 to B2 at time t*. Result (derivation): the gap at the switch is pure noise accumulation, eta*sigma^2 (1/B1 - 1/B2); after a further delta it decays as gap x delta^(-(1-1/beta)), independent of s; the time to come within a factor 1 + epsilon of the large-batch curve scales as t*^(s/(1-1/beta)), much shorter than t* when s < 1 - 1/beta, so harder tasks catch up faster. The same catch-up shape appears in a simulated hard task (s = 0.3, beta = 1.5).

Observe catch-up in LLM pretraining. Setup: LLaMA-style dense 0.5B on C4 (NanoGPT, 512 to 1,024 / 2,048 / 4,096 at step 25k of 100k); shortcut-connected MoE 1B (209M active) on about 0.4T private tokens (640 to 1,280 or 2,560 at 50B, 200B or 300B tokens, and a four-stage 640 / 1,280 / 1,920 / 2,560 schedule); MoE 1.1B (291M active) on 1T tokens (1,024 to 2,048 at 300B or 600B); AdamW, beta2 = 0.95, weight decay 0.1. Result: after each switch the validation loss collapses quickly onto the constant-large-batch curve, including after every stage of the four-stage schedule (figures).

Locate the best switch and test late switching. Setup: 200M dense on 4B tokens, batch 256 to 512 switched at each 1/16 of the data with repeats; 50M dense with batch 128 to 256 over budgets from 1.3B to 5B tokens, grid-searching the optimal switch (precision D/32); late versus early switches at the larger scales and in three- and four-stage schedules. Result: final loss is lowest when switching at about 70% of training tokens; log(D - P*) against log D is linear with R^2 = 0.990; late switching gives lower validation loss than early switching across switch ratios, architectures and scales, and in multi-stage schedules (figures only for these comparisons).

Note the gap between theory and experiments. Setup: the theory assumes SGD with a constant learning rate, while all LLM runs use AdamW, 1,000 warmup steps and, in an extension, cosine decay; the large-scale MoE runs use a private dataset; most LLM comparisons are single curves read off figures. With cosine decay (50M and 0.5B dense) catch-up and the late-switch advantage persist approximately but merging slows near the end, which the authors attribute to intrinsic time advancing more slowly. The constant-LR + batch schedule matching cosine and WSD in the 50M model used a heuristic, untuned schedule (2x at 70%, 4x at 80%, 8x at 90% of tokens).
